title: USCIS Restores Power to Deny Incomplete Applications Without Warning
excerpt: A restored policy and a new signature rule give immigration officers broader authority to reject filings outright, ending the era of routine Requests for Evidence.
body:
• USCIS has restored adjudicators' full discretion to deny immigration applications outright — without first issuing a Request for Evidence (RFE) or Notice of Intent to Deny (NOID) — when filings are incomplete or lack a legal basis.
  • A separate interim final rule, effective July 10, 2026, allows USCIS to deny even previously accepted petitions if signatures are later found to be invalid, with filing fees forfeited.
  • The combined policies mark a sharp departure from the Obama-era guidance that required officers to issue RFEs before denying most cases, and directly target "placeholder" filings common in H-1B cap season.
  • Immigration attorneys are urging employers and applicants to conduct thorough document audits before filing, as the margin for error has narrowed significantly.

No More Second Chances on Incomplete Filings

U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services has formally restored its officers' authority to deny applications and petitions without first requesting additional evidence, a policy shift that removes the safety net many applicants had relied on for years. Under the restored guidance, an adjudicator can reject a filing outright if it includes little or no supporting evidence, omits required official documents, or seeks a benefit under a program that no longer exists.

The policy effectively reverses Obama-era memoranda that had directed officers to issue Requests for Evidence before denying most cases. USCIS has framed the change as a measure to discourage "placeholder" filings — skeletal applications submitted to secure a filing date or lottery slot, with the expectation that missing documents could be supplied later through an RFE.

Signature Crackdown Adds Another Layer

Compounding the risk for applicants, USCIS published an interim final rule on May 11, 2026, that formally authorizes officers to deny an immigration benefit even after the application has been accepted for processing, if the signature is later found to be deficient. The rule, which became effective on July 10, classifies invalid signatures to include photocopies, software-generated e-signatures when not expressly permitted by form instructions, and signatures executed by unauthorized persons.

Unlike a rejection — which returns the packet and fee — a denial is a final adjudicative action. USCIS keeps the filing fee, and the applicant may face gaps in status, lost priority dates, and the need to refile from scratch. For employment-based cases, that can translate to months or years of lost progress and thousands of dollars in duplicate legal costs.

"The legal requirement is not merely disclosure, but explicit and affirmative consumer consent."

— CCPA, in a ruling that mirrors USCIS's own shift toward demanding explicit compliance over assumed good faith

Who Is Most Affected

The policies hit hardest for employers running high-volume H-1B, L-1, or employment-based green card petitions. Companies that relied on digital signature workflows — common during and after the pandemic — now need to ensure that every signer has proper company authority and that original wet-signed pages are retained for potential audits. Foreign nationals filing from abroad must verify that consular e-signatures meet USCIS's narrow definition before submitting packets.

The timing is particularly acute for H-1B cap season filings, where the volume of applications creates pressure to submit quickly. Immigration attorneys warn that placeholder filings — once a common strategy to secure a lottery slot while gathering documents — now carry the risk of an outright denial with fees forfeited and no opportunity to supplement the record.

What Applicants Should Do

Immigration lawyers are advising a back-to-basics approach: complete every filing as if no RFE will be issued, retain original wet signatures, audit document-control procedures, and avoid shortcuts in signature workflows. For H-1B extensions and transfers, where the proposed fee increases under a separate rulemaking could push costs even higher, the financial stakes of a preventable denial have never been greater.

The combined effect of these policy changes is a system with significantly less tolerance for error. For the millions of Indian-origin workers navigating the U.S. immigration system — the largest H-1B applicant pool by far — the message is clear: file right the first time, or risk losing both your money and your place in line.
